topic: Normal TSH, but have your thyroid antibodies ever been tested?
angle: TSH shows how hard the thyroid is pushed, not whether autoimmunity (Hashimoto's) is present; antibodies are common and not a diagnosis of failure, but they mean yearly TSH monitoring; what to ask your doctor
hook: Has anyone ever tested your thyroid antibodies? Many women I work with have only ever had a TSH.
draft:
Has anyone ever tested your thyroid antibodies? Many women I work with have only ever had a TSH.

TSH is a good first test. It's a signal from your brain telling the thyroid to work harder. When the thyroid struggles, TSH goes up.

But TSH only tells you how hard the thyroid is being pushed. It doesn't tell you why it might be struggling.

A 2022 review in the Polish Archives of Internal Medicine puts it plainly. Anti-TPO antibodies, the marker of Hashimoto's, are present in about 95% of people with it. And you can have the antibodies while your TSH and T4 are still normal.

Before you panic: antibodies are common. The same review says 15 to 25% of people test positive, far more than ever develop the disease.

What it changes is how closely you watch. The review recommends a yearly TSH for people with antibodies and normal thyroid levels, because antibodies are a risk factor for hypothyroidism over time.

In my practice I also retest. A negative result once isn't negative forever. I've had a client test negative, then positive at a later retest.

If your thyroid has only ever been checked with TSH, ask your doctor whether an anti-TPO test makes sense for you, and how often to recheck.

#Hashimotos #ThyroidHealth
final:
Has anyone ever tested your thyroid antibodies? Many women I work with have only ever had a TSH.

TSH is a sensible first test. It's the signal your brain sends to push the thyroid to work harder, so it goes up when the thyroid is struggling.

What it can't show is whether your immune system has started attacking the thyroid. That's Hashimoto's, and it has its own blood test, anti-TPO antibodies.

A 2022 review in the Polish Archives of Internal Medicine says these antibodies are present in about 95% of people with Hashimoto's. It also describes people who have them while their TSH and T4 are still normal.

Positive antibodies are common, though. The same review puts it at 15 to 25% of people, far more than ever develop the disease. A positive result on its own doesn't mean your thyroid is failing.

It does mean watching more closely. The review recommends a TSH test every year for people with antibodies and normal thyroid levels, because the antibodies raise the risk of hypothyroidism over time.

I retest with my clients as well. One of them had negative antibodies at first and positive ones at a later retest.

If your thyroid has only ever been checked with a TSH, ask your doctor whether an anti-TPO test makes sense for you, and how often to recheck it.

#Hashimotos #ThyroidHealth
